beats.narration: Exposure is not one brightness dial. It is the combined result of aperture, shutter speed, and ISO. If one setting admits or records less light, another may need to compensate. The useful question is not only whether the image is bright enough, but what visual trade-off each setting creates.
beats.title: Balance three controls
beats.visualDirection: template:showcase-exposure | Place aperture, shutter speed, and ISO at the corners of a balanced exposure triangle.

beats.delivery: Professional, concise, and paced for an introductory course audience.
beats.narration: A wider aperture admits more light and can produce shallower depth of field. A narrower aperture admits less light and can keep more of the scene in focus. A fast shutter can freeze motion; a slow shutter records motion across time. These are creative decisions as well as exposure decisions.
beats.title: Choose motion and depth
beats.visualDirection: template:showcase-exposure | Compare wide and narrow apertures beside fast and slow shutter examples.

beats.delivery: Professional, concise, and paced for an introductory course audience.
beats.narration: When depth of field and motion already determine aperture and shutter speed, ISO can help reach a usable brightness. Raising it can also make noise more visible and reduce image quality. Start from the look the photograph needs, then balance the three controls instead of treating any one setting as automatically correct.

claims.text: Aperture, shutter speed, and ISO work together to control photographic exposure.
Aperture affects depth of field, while shutter speed affects how motion is rendered.
ISO can help achieve a usable exposure when aperture and shutter constraints are fixed, but higher settings can increase visible noise.

sources.author: Adobe
sources.excerpt: Photographic exposure is controlled through aperture, shutter speed, and ISO. Aperture changes the opening that admits light and also affects depth of field. Shutter speed controls how long light reaches the sensor and changes the appearance of motion. ISO changes the camera's sensitivity or signal amplification and can affect visible noise. The settings work together, so changing one may require compensation with another for a similar brightness.
